questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 128(1) · Basis and system of accounting
questions.stem: Section 128(1) of the Companies Act 2013 requires the books of account of every company to be kept:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 128(1)

readLink.label: Read: Books of account — s. 128 →

options.text: On cash basis and according to the single entry system of accounting
options.explanation: Neither limb is right. The section names accrual basis and double entry; single entry is not permitted to a company at all.

options.text: On accrual basis and according to the double entry system of accounting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 128(1) prescribes both: accrual basis and the double entry system, for the books kept at the registered office and for those of the branches.

options.text: On accrual basis, the system of book-keeping being left to the Board to decide
options.explanation: The Board has a discretion about the PLACE where the books are kept, not about the SYSTEM. Double entry is statutory.

options.text: On cash basis and according to the double entry system of accounting
options.explanation: The system is right but the basis is wrong. Cash basis would defeat the true and fair view the same sub-section demands.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 128(1) proviso · Books at another place
questions.stem: A company decides to keep its books of account at a place other than its registered office. Which statement reflects the first proviso to section 128(1)?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, first proviso to s. 128(1)

readLink.label: Read: Books of account — s. 128 →

options.text: The Board of Directors may decide on any other place in India, and the company must file with the Registrar a notice in writing giving the full address of that other place within seven days of the decision
options.explanation: Correct. Three elements — a Board decision, a place in India, and written notice of the full address to the Registrar within seven days of the decision.

options.text: The other place may be anywhere in the world, and no intimation to the Registrar is required
options.explanation: Both limbs fail. The proviso says 'such other place in India', and it expressly requires a notice to the Registrar.

options.text: The members must approve the other place by special resolution, and notice must be filed within thirty days
options.explanation: No members' resolution is involved, and the period is seven days, not thirty. Thirty days is the s. 137 filing clock.

options.text: The previous approval of the Central Government is required before the books may be moved
options.explanation: The Central Government has no role. Its only appearance in s. 128 is the direction under the proviso to s. 128(5) to preserve books for longer than eight years.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 128(2) · Branch offices
questions.stem: Vasudha Exports Limited has a branch office at Colombo. Section 128(2) is complied with if:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 128(2)

readLink.label: Read: Books of account — s. 128 →

options.text: All the branch ledgers are physically transported to the registered office at the end of every quarter
options.explanation: The sub-section requires no such thing. Only summarised returns travel; the branch keeps its own books.

options.text: Proper books of account relating to the transactions effected at the branch office are kept at that office and proper summarised returns are sent periodically by the branch to the company at its registered office or at the other place decided under section 128(1)
options.explanation: Correct. Section 128(2) applies to a branch in India or outside India, and is satisfied by proper books at the branch plus periodic summarised returns.

options.text: The branch maintains no books at all, every entry being made at the registered office
options.explanation: That would breach the requirement that proper books relating to the branch's transactions be kept at that office.

options.text: The branch books are kept at the branch and no returns are required, the statutory auditor visiting the branch annually
options.explanation: An audit visit is not a substitute for the periodic summarised returns the sub-section requires.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 128(5) · Preservation of books
questions.stem: Aranyaka Speciality Foods Limited is in its financial year 2026-27. Under section 128(5), the earliest financial year whose books of account and the vouchers relevant to entries in them must be kept in good order is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 128(5) — eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year

readLink.label: Read: Books of account — s. 128 →

options.explanation: That is ten financial years back. The section names eight.
That is nine financial years back — the standard off-by-one, produced by counting the current year 2026-27 as one of the eight.
Correct. The eight financial years immediately preceding 2026-27 run from 2025-26 back to 2018-19, so 2018-19 is the earliest year that must be preserved.
That is only seven financial years back. Counting stops one year short.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 128(3) · Inspection of books
questions.stem: Under section 128(3), the books of account and other books and papers maintained by a company within India are open for inspection:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 128(3)

readLink.label: Read: Books of account — s. 128 →

options.text: By any member of the company at the registered office during business hours
options.explanation: A member has rights over the register of members, the minutes of general meetings and the copies under s. 136 — not over the books of account.

options.text: By any director at any hour of the day or night, and by an agent authorised by him in writing
options.explanation: The right is exercisable during business hours, and it is the director's own right; the section does not provide for inspection by his agent.

options.text: By the statutory auditor alone, a director having no separate statutory right of inspection
options.explanation: The auditor's right of access comes from s. 143. Section 128(3) confers a distinct right on directors.

options.text: By any director of the company, at the registered office or at the other place in India where the books are kept, during business hours
options.explanation: Correct. That is s. 128(3); and where financial information is maintained outside the country, copies of it must be maintained and produced for a director's inspection on the prescribed conditions.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 128(1) proviso · Seven-day notice
questions.stem: The Board of Sahyadri Ceramics Limited resolves on 18 September 2026 to keep the company's books of account at a place in India other than its registered office. The last date for filing with the Registrar the notice giving the full address of that other place is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, first proviso to s. 128(1) — seven days from the Board's decision

readLink.label: Read: Books of account — s. 128 →

options.text: 25 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Seven days counted from (and excluding) 18 September 2026 ends on 25 September 2026.

options.text: 24 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts the day of the resolution itself as day one — the usual off-by-one.

options.text: 3 October 2026
options.explanation: That is fifteen days. No fifteen-day period appears anywhere in s. 128.

options.text: 18 October 2026
options.explanation: That is thirty days, which is the s. 137 filing clock, not the s. 128 notice clock.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 129(1) · Requirements of financial statements
questions.stem: Under section 129(1), the financial statements of a company must, apart from giving a true and fair view of the state of its affairs:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 129(1)

readLink.label: Read: Financial statements — ss. 129 and 129A →

options.text: Comply with the accounting standards notified under section 133 and be in the form or forms provided for different classes of companies in Schedule III
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the second and third limbs of s. 129(1); the proviso disapplies the Schedule III form to insurance, banking and electricity companies and others governed by a special Act.

options.text: Comply with the auditing standards notified under section 143 and be in the form provided in Schedule II
options.explanation: Auditing standards bind the auditor, not the statements; and Schedule II deals with useful lives for depreciation.

options.text: Comply with the accounting standards recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and be in the form provided in Schedule I
options.explanation: The Institute recommends; the Central Government prescribes under s. 133. Schedule I contains the model memorandum and articles.

options.text: Be in such form as the Board of Directors considers appropriate, no statutory form being prescribed
options.explanation: Schedule III prescribes the form. The Board has no discretion over it.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 129(5) · Deviation from accounting standards
questions.stem: Where a company's financial statements do not comply with the accounting standards, section 129(5) requires the company to disclose in its financial statements:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 129(5)

readLink.label: Read: Financial statements — ss. 129 and 129A →

options.text: Only the fact of the deviation
options.explanation: The sub-section names three things, not one. Bare disclosure of the fact is not compliance.

options.text: Nothing, provided the Central Government has granted an exemption under section 129(6)
options.explanation: A s. 129(6) exemption is a separate matter, granted in the public interest on conditions; it is not triggered by the company's own non-compliance.

options.text: The deviation and the auditor's opinion on it, the reasons being treated as confidential
options.explanation: The reasons are expressly required to be disclosed, and the auditor's opinion is not part of this disclosure.

options.text: The deviation, the reasons for the deviation and the financial effects, if any, arising from it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 129(5) requires all three. Disclosure is the price of non-compliance, not a cure for it.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 129(3) Explanation · Associates and joint ventures
questions.stem: Hemadri Industries Limited has no subsidiary, but it holds a stake giving it significant influence in one associate company and is a party to one joint venture. In relation to consolidated financial statements under section 129(3):
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 129(3) and the Explanation to it

readLink.label: Read: Financial statements — ss. 129 and 129A →

options.text: No consolidation is required, section 129(3) applying only where the company has a subsidiary
options.explanation: The sub-section itself speaks of 'one or more subsidiaries or associate companies', and the Explanation goes further.

options.text: Consolidation is required only for the joint venture, an associate company being outside section 129(3)
options.explanation: The Explanation names both. Associates are inside the obligation.

options.text: Consolidation is required, because the Explanation to section 129(3) provides that the word 'subsidiary' includes an associate company and a joint venture
options.explanation: Correct. The Explanation is what decides this question, and the salient-features statement must be attached for each such entity.

options.text: Consolidation is optional, being a matter for the Board of Directors to decide
options.explanation: Section 129(3) is mandatory in terms — the company 'shall' prepare a consolidated financial statement. Exemptions, where they exist, are rules-level, not a Board discretion.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 129(3) proviso · Salient-features statement
questions.stem: The statement containing the salient features of the financial statement of a company's subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures, required to be attached under the proviso to section 129(3), is in:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, proviso to s. 129(3) read with the Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Financial statements — ss. 129 and 129A →

options.text: Form AOC-1
options.explanation: Correct. AOC-1 is the salient-features statement attached to the financial statements under the proviso to s. 129(3).

options.text: Form AOC-2
options.explanation: AOC-2 carries the particulars of contracts or arrangements with related parties under s. 188(1), disclosed in the Board's report.

options.text: Form AOC-4
options.explanation: AOC-4 is the form in which the financial statements are FILED with the Registrar under s. 137.

options.text: Form MGT-9
options.explanation: MGT-9 was the extract of the annual return formerly annexed to the Board's report; that requirement has been replaced by the web address under s. 134(3)(a).

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 129(7) · Persons liable
questions.stem: For a contravention of section 129, the persons liable under section 129(7) are:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 129(7)

readLink.label: Read: Financial statements — ss. 129 and 129A →

options.text: The company alone, by way of a monetary penalty
options.explanation: Section 129(7) fastens on individuals. It does not name the company at all.

options.text: Every member of the company who voted to adopt the accounts at the annual general meeting
options.explanation: Members are never made liable for the form or content of the accounts; the duty to prepare them is the Board's.

options.text: The managing director, the whole-time director in charge of finance, the Chief Financial Officer, any other person charged by the Board with the duty of complying, and in the absence of any of them, all the directors
options.explanation: Correct. That cascade — the named officers first, all the directors only in their absence — is the structure of s. 129(7).

options.text: The statutory auditor and the members of the audit committee
options.explanation: The auditor's liability arises under Chapter X, not under s. 129(7).

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 129A · Periodical financial results
questions.stem: Section 129A empowers the Central Government, in consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority, to require prescribed classes of:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 129A

readLink.label: Read: Financial statements — ss. 129 and 129A →

options.text: Listed companies to publish quarterly results within forty-five days of the end of each quarter
options.explanation: Quarterly publication by listed companies is governed by the SEBI listing regulations, not by s. 129A.

options.text: Unlisted companies to prepare periodical financial results, obtain the Board's approval, have them audited or subjected to a limited review, and file them with the Registrar within thirty days of the end of the relevant period
options.explanation: Correct. Section 129A is aimed at UNLISTED companies and has exactly those four limbs.

options.text: Government companies to prepare monthly accounts for submission to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
options.explanation: No such requirement exists in s. 129A; the CAG's powers over Government companies arise under s. 143.

options.text: Small companies to prepare abridged financial statements in the prescribed form
options.explanation: The abridged statement is a rules-level concept under ss. 134(3A) and 136, not the subject of s. 129A.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 130 · Who may apply
questions.stem: An application for re-opening a company's books of account and re-casting its financial statements under section 130 may be made by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 130(1)

readLink.label: Read: Reopening and revision — ss. 130 and 131 →

options.text: The Board of Directors of the company itself
options.explanation: The Board cannot re-open its own books. Its only route is a voluntary revision under s. 131, and even that needs the Tribunal's approval.

options.text: The statutory auditor of the company alone
options.explanation: The auditor is not among the applicants named in s. 130(1).

options.text: Any member holding not less than ten per cent of the paid-up share capital, and no one else
options.explanation: There is no such shareholding qualification in s. 130; the ten per cent threshold belongs to other provisions of the Act.

options.text: The Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board, any other statutory regulatory body or authority, or any person concerned
options.explanation: Correct. That is the list in s. 130(1), and the closing words 'any person concerned' are deliberately wide.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 130 · Grounds and finality
questions.stem: Which statement about an order under section 130 is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 130(1) and (2)

readLink.label: Read: Reopening and revision — ss. 130 and 131 →

options.text: The order may be made by a court of competent jurisdiction or by the Tribunal, on the ground that the relevant earlier accounts were prepared in a fraudulent manner or that the affairs of the company were mismanaged during the relevant period casting a doubt on the reliability of the financial statements; and the accounts so revised or re-cast are final
options.explanation: Correct. Two forums, two grounds, and s. 130(2) makes the revised or re-cast accounts final.

options.text: The order may be made only by the Central Government, and the revised accounts remain open to further revision
options.explanation: The Central Government is an applicant, not the forum; and s. 130(2) makes the revised accounts final.

options.text: The order may be made on the sole ground that the accounts contain an arithmetical error
options.explanation: An arithmetical error is neither fraud nor mismanagement. A defect of that kind is dealt with, if at all, by a voluntary revision under s. 131.

options.text: The order may be made without notice to the income-tax authorities, whose interests are unaffected
options.explanation: The proviso requires notice to the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, SEBI or any other statutory regulatory body concerned and any other person concerned, and consideration of their representations.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 131 · Voluntary revision
questions.stem: Under section 131, where it appears to the directors that the financial statement or the report of the Board does not comply with section 129 or section 134, they may prepare a revised financial statement or a revised report:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 131(1) and its proviso

readLink.label: Read: Reopening and revision — ss. 130 and 131 →

options.text: For any of the eight preceding financial years, with the approval of the Tribunal, without any limit as to frequency
options.explanation: Eight financial years is the s. 130 look-back for re-opening. Section 131 reaches back three, and is limited to once in a financial year.

options.text: For any of the three preceding financial years, with the approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: The approving authority under s. 131 is the Tribunal. The Central Government only receives notice of the application.

options.text: For the immediately preceding financial year only, by a resolution of the Board, no approval being required
options.explanation: Both limbs fail: the window is three preceding financial years, and the Tribunal's approval is indispensable.

options.text: For any of the three preceding financial years, after obtaining the approval of the Tribunal on an application made by the company, and not more than once in a financial year
options.explanation: Correct. Three preceding financial years, NCLT approval, and the proviso's once-a-year limit; the detailed reasons must also be disclosed in the Board's report of the year of revision.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 131(2) · Scope of a revision
questions.stem: Where copies of the previous financial statement have already been sent to the members and delivered to the Registrar, a revision under section 131 must be confined to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 131(2)

readLink.label: Read: Reopening and revision — ss. 130 and 131 →

options.text: Any change that the Board of Directors considers desirable in the interests of the company
options.explanation: Section 131 is a correction mechanism, not an opportunity to redraft the accounts.

options.text: The correction in respect of which the previous financial statement or report did not comply with section 129 or section 134, and the making of any necessary consequential alteration
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the two limbs of s. 131(2), and they are exhaustive once the earlier documents have gone out.

options.text: Changes to the notes on accounts, the primary statements being unalterable
options.explanation: No such distinction appears in the section; the correction may touch the primary statements if that is where the non-compliance lies.

options.text: Changes recommended by the statutory auditor in a revised audit report
options.explanation: The trigger is the directors' own view that s. 129 or s. 134 was not complied with, not an auditor's recommendation.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 132 · Constitution of NFRA
questions.stem: The National Financial Reporting Authority constituted under section 132 consists of:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 132(3)

readLink.label: Read: NFRA and accounting standards — ss. 132 and 133 →

options.text: A chairperson, being a person of eminence having expertise in accountancy, auditing, finance or law, appointed by the Central Government, and such other members not exceeding fifteen
options.explanation: Correct. The chairperson's qualification and the ceiling of fifteen other members are both in the section.

options.text: A chairperson nominated by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and not more than nine members
options.explanation: The Institute does not appoint the chairperson; the Central Government does. And the ceiling is fifteen.

options.text: Three members appointed by the Tribunal
options.explanation: The Tribunal has no role in constituting NFRA. Its only connection is that appeals from NFRA lie to the Appellate Tribunal.

options.text: A chairperson appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and such other members not exceeding twenty-five
options.explanation: Both the appointing authority and the number are wrong.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 132 · Powers of NFRA
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT within the powers of the National Financial Reporting Authority under section 132?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 132(2) and (4); s. 133

readLink.label: Read: NFRA and accounting standards — ss. 132 and 133 →

options.text: Investigating, either on its own motion or on a reference made to it by the Central Government, into matters of professional or other misconduct committed by a member or firm of chartered accountants registered under the Chartered Accountants Act 1949
options.explanation: This is expressly conferred by s. 132(4)(a); and once NFRA has initiated such proceedings no other institute or body may initiate or continue proceedings in the same matter.

options.text: Exercising the same powers as are vested in a civil court in respect of discovery, production of documents, summoning and examining persons on oath, and inspection of books and records
options.explanation: Section 132(4)(b) gives NFRA exactly these civil-court powers for the purposes of an investigation.

options.text: Debarring a member or a firm from being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, or from undertaking any audit, for a minimum of six months and a maximum of ten years, where professional or other misconduct is proved
options.explanation: This is the non-monetary consequence available under s. 132(4)(B), alongside a monetary penalty.

options.text: Notifying the standards of accounting to be followed by companies, in supersession of the Central Government's power under section 133
options.explanation: Correct. This is the odd one out: NFRA does not notify accounting standards. It only makes recommendations and is consulted, the standards being prescribed by the Central Government under s. 133.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 133 · Power to prescribe accounting standards
questions.stem: Under section 133, the standards of accounting, or any addendum to them, are prescribed by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 133

readLink.label: Read: NFRA and accounting standards — ss. 132 and 133 →

options.text: The National Financial Reporting Authority, on the recommendation of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
options.explanation: NFRA is consulted and its recommendations are examined, but it does not prescribe.

options.text: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, in consultation with the Central Government
options.explanation: The order is reversed. The Institute recommends; the Central Government prescribes.

options.text: The Central Government, as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the National Financial Reporting Authority
options.explanation: Correct. The chain is ICAI recommends, NFRA is consulted and its recommendations examined, and the Central Government prescribes.

options.text: The Central Government, on the recommendation of the Tribunal
options.explanation: The Tribunal has no role in standard-setting.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 134(1) · Signing of financial statements
questions.stem: The financial statements of a public company, including the consolidated financial statement, are to be approved by the Board and then signed on behalf of the Board at least by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 134(1)

readLink.label: Read: Signing and the Board report — s. 134 →

options.text: Any two directors of the company
options.explanation: Two directors are not enough on their own. One of them must be the managing director, and the CEO (if a director), the CFO and the company secretary must also sign wherever they are appointed.

options.text: The chairperson of the company where he is authorised by the Board, or by two directors of whom one shall be the managing director, and the Chief Executive Officer if he is a director, the Chief Financial Officer and the company secretary, wherever they are appointed
options.explanation: Correct. The chairperson may sign alone only if the Board has authorised him; otherwise two directors including the managing director, plus the named key managerial personnel wherever appointed.

options.text: The managing director and the statutory auditor of the company
options.explanation: The auditor never signs the financial statements. He signs his own report, which is attached to them under s. 134(2).

options.text: All the directors who were present at the Board meeting at which the accounts were approved
options.explanation: Section 134(1) prescribes a minimum set of signatories, not signature by everyone present.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 134(1) proviso · One Person Company
questions.stem: In the case of a One Person Company, the financial statements are to be signed by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, proviso to s. 134(1)

readLink.label: Read: Signing and the Board report — s. 134 →

options.text: Two directors, one of whom shall be the managing director
options.explanation: That is the ordinary rule for other companies. The proviso relaxes it for an OPC, which may have a single director.

options.text: The sole member of the company, whether or not he is a director
options.explanation: The signature is on behalf of the Board. Membership as such confers no power to sign the accounts.

options.text: Only one director
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 134(1) requires the financial statements of a One Person Company to be signed by only one director.

options.text: One director and a company secretary in practice
options.explanation: A practising company secretary certifies certain filings; he does not sign the financial statements.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 134(3)(a) · Annual return in the Board's report
questions.stem: Which of the following must the Board's report under section 134(3) contain in relation to the annual return?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 134(3)(a) read with s. 92(3)

readLink.label: Read: Signing and the Board report — s. 134 →

options.text: An extract of the annual return in Form MGT-9, annexed to the report
options.explanation: That was the position before the clause was substituted. The extract in MGT-9 is no longer required and is a favourite distractor.

options.text: A certificate from a company secretary in practice that the annual return has been duly filed
options.explanation: The secretarial certification of the annual return is a separate requirement under s. 92; it is not a content of the Board's report under clause (a).

options.text: The web address, if any, where the annual return referred to in section 92(3) has been placed
options.explanation: Correct. Clause (a) now requires only the web address at which the annual return has been placed.

options.text: A complete copy of the annual return, certified by two directors
options.explanation: No copy of the annual return is annexed to the Board's report.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 134(5) · Directors' Responsibility Statement
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the matters that the Directors' Responsibility Statement under section 134(5) must state?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 134(5)

readLink.label: Read: Signing and the Board report — s. 134 →

options.text: That in the preparation of the annual accounts the applicable accounting standards had been followed, with proper explanation relating to material departures
options.explanation: This is clause (a) of s. 134(5).

options.text: That the directors had taken proper and sufficient care for the maintenance of adequate accounting records in accordance with the Act for safeguarding the assets of the company and for preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities
options.explanation: This is clause (c) of s. 134(5).

options.text: That, in the case of a listed company, the directors had laid down internal financial controls to be followed by the company and that such controls are adequate and were operating effectively
options.explanation: This is clause (e) of s. 134(5), which applies to listed companies.

options.text: That the directors had ensured that the company spent the whole of its corporate social responsibility obligation during the financial year
options.explanation: Correct. This is the odd one out. The CSR disclosure is a separate content of the Board's report under s. 134(3)(o) and s. 135; it forms no part of the Directors' Responsibility Statement, and a shortfall is dealt with by the transfer and penalty machinery of s. 135.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 134(6) · Signing of the Board's report
questions.stem: The Board's report and any annexures to it are to be signed by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 134(6)

readLink.label: Read: Signing and the Board report — s. 134 →

options.text: The chairperson of the company if he is authorised by the Board; where he is not so authorised, by at least two directors one of whom shall be a managing director, or by the director where there is only one director
options.explanation: Correct. Note that no signature by the Chief Financial Officer or the company secretary is required on the report, unlike the financial statements under s. 134(1).

options.text: The chairperson, the Chief Financial Officer and the company secretary in every case
options.explanation: That mixes up s. 134(6) with the signature rule for the financial statements in s. 134(1).

options.text: All the directors of the company
options.explanation: Section 134(6) prescribes a minimum, not signature by the whole Board.

options.text: The managing director and the statutory auditor of the company
options.explanation: The auditor does not sign the Board's report; the Board in fact has to comment in that report on any qualification in the auditor's report.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(1) · CSR applicability
questions.stem: Section 135(1) applies to every company having, during the immediately preceding financial year:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(1)

readLink.label: Read: Corporate social responsibility — s. 135 →

options.text: Net worth of ₹500 crore or more, turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more and net profit of ₹5 crore or more, all three conditions being cumulative
options.explanation: The section uses 'or', not 'and'. Any one threshold brings the company inside s. 135.

options.text: Net worth of ₹100 crore or more, or turnover of ₹500 crore or more, or net profit of ₹1 crore or more
options.explanation: All three figures are wrong. The statutory figures are ₹500 crore, ₹1,000 crore and ₹5 crore.

options.text: Turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, computed as the average of the three immediately preceding financial years
options.explanation: The three-year average belongs to the QUANTUM under s. 135(5), not to applicability, and applicability is tested on one preceding year only.

options.text: Net worth of ₹500 crore or more, or turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more
options.explanation: Correct. Three alternative criteria, each tested on the figures of the immediately preceding financial year.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(1) · Threshold test
questions.stem: For the financial year 2025-26 — its immediately preceding financial year — Ojaswi Polymers Limited had a net worth of ₹420 crore, a turnover of ₹880 crore and a net profit of ₹6.20 crore. In relation to section 135:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(1) — net worth ₹500 crore / turnover ₹1,000 crore / net profit ₹5 crore

readLink.label: Read: Corporate social responsibility — s. 135 →

options.text: Section 135 does not apply, none of the three thresholds having been crossed
options.explanation: One threshold was crossed. The net profit of ₹6.20 crore exceeds ₹5 crore.

options.text: Section 135 applies, the net-profit criterion of ₹5 crore having been crossed
options.explanation: Correct. ₹6.20 crore is above the ₹5 crore net-profit threshold, and since the three criteria are alternatives that is enough by itself.

options.text: Section 135 applies, the net-worth criterion of ₹500 crore having been crossed
options.explanation: The net worth is ₹420 crore, which is below ₹500 crore. The right answer identifies the right limb.

options.text: Section 135 applies, the turnover criterion of ₹1,000 crore having been crossed
options.explanation: The turnover is ₹880 crore, which is below ₹1,000 crore.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(5) · Two per cent computation
questions.stem: Section 135 applies to Nandini Alloys Limited. Its net profits computed in accordance with section 198 were ₹8.40 crore for 2023-24, ₹11.10 crore for 2024-25 and ₹6.30 crore for 2025-26. Its corporate social responsibility obligation for the financial year 2026-27 is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(5) — 2% of the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years

readLink.label: Read: CSR spend, unspent amounts and penalty →

options.explanation: Correct. The three-year total is ₹25.80 crore, the average ₹8.60 crore, and 2% of ₹8,60,00,000 is ₹17,20,000.
This is 2% of the latest year's net profit alone. The section requires the average of three years.
This is 2% of the TOTAL of the three years, which is three times the correct figure — effectively a 6% spend.
This is 1% of the average. The statutory rate is two per cent.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(1) proviso · CSR Committee composition
questions.stem: Trishula Metals Private Limited is required to constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee and is not required to appoint an independent director under section 149(4). Its CSR Committee must consist of:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, first proviso to s. 135(1)

readLink.label: Read: Corporate social responsibility — s. 135 →

options.text: Three or more directors, at least one of whom must be an independent director
options.explanation: That is the default rule. It is displaced by the proviso where the company is not required to appoint an independent director.

options.text: Two or more directors
options.explanation: Correct. The first proviso to s. 135(1) reduces the committee to two or more directors where the company is not required to appoint an independent director under s. 149(4); and a private company having only two directors constitutes the committee with those two.

options.text: The whole Board of Directors, no smaller committee being permitted
options.explanation: No such rule exists. What the Act does provide, in s. 135(9), is that where the amount to be spent does not exceed ₹50 lakh no committee is needed and the Board discharges its functions.

options.text: Three or more directors, at least one of whom must be a director resident in India
options.explanation: The resident-director requirement belongs to s. 149(3) and has nothing to do with the composition of the CSR Committee.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(6) · Unspent CSR Account clock
questions.stem: The financial year of Rukmini Foods Limited ends on 31 March 2027. An amount of ₹6,00,000 remains unspent in respect of an ongoing project. The last date for transferring that amount to the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(6) — 30 days from the end of the financial year

readLink.label: Read: CSR spend, unspent amounts and penalty →

options.text: 30 June 2027
options.explanation: That is three calendar months from the end of the financial year. Section 135(6) allows thirty days.

options.text: 30 April 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days counted from the end of the financial year, 31 March 2027, ends on 30 April 2027.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: That is the six-month clock, which applies to unspent amounts NOT relating to an ongoing project and sends the money to a Fund specified in Schedule VII.

options.text: 29 April 2027
options.explanation: This counts 31 March itself as day one — the usual off-by-one.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(5) 2nd proviso · Schedule VII Fund clock
questions.stem: The financial year of Rukmini Foods Limited ends on 31 March 2027. Of its corporate social responsibility obligation for that year, ₹2,00,000 remains unspent and is not attributable to any ongoing project. It must be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, second proviso to s. 135(5) — 6 months from the expiry of the financial year

readLink.label: Read: CSR spend, unspent amounts and penalty →

options.text: 30 April 2027
options.explanation: That is the thirty-day clock, which applies only to an amount relating to an ongoing project and only to a transfer into the company's own Unspent CSR Account.

options.text: 1 October 2027
options.explanation: Six calendar months from 31 March 2027 lands on 30 September 2027, the last day of that month, not on 1 October.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Six months from the expiry of the financial year on 31 March 2027, the day being clamped to the last day of September.

options.text: 31 March 2028
options.explanation: That is a full year. No twelve-month period appears in s. 135.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(6) · The three-year spending window
questions.stem: An amount transferred to the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account in respect of the financial year 2026-27, which ended on 31 March 2027, remains unspent throughout the period allowed by section 135(6). The last date for transferring it to a Fund specified in Schedule VII is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(6) — 3 financial years, then 30 days from the completion of the third financial year

readLink.label: Read: CSR spend, unspent amounts and penalty →

options.text: 30 April 2029
options.explanation: That allows only two financial years for the spending. The section allows three.

options.text: 30 September 2030
options.explanation: This mistakenly applies the six-month clock of the second proviso to s. 135(5); the tail-end transfer under s. 135(6) is a thirty-day clock.

options.text: 30 April 2031
options.explanation: This counts four financial years — 2027-28, 2028-29, 2029-30 and 2030-31 — instead of three.

options.text: 30 April 2030
options.explanation: Correct. The three financial years are 2027-28, 2028-29 and 2029-30, the third completing on 31 March 2030; thirty days from then is 30 April 2030.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135(7) · Penalty on the company
questions.stem: Vaidehi Textiles Limited was required to transfer ₹68,00,000 to a Fund specified in Schedule VII and transferred nothing. The penalty on the company under section 135(7) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(7)

readLink.label: Read: CSR spend, unspent amounts and penalty →

options.explanation: This is twice the unspent amount, but it ignores the cap. The company's penalty is twice the amount OR ₹1 crore, whichever is LESS.
Correct. Twice ₹68,00,000 is ₹1,36,00,000; the statutory cap of ₹1 crore is lower, so ₹1,00,00,000 is payable.
That is the unspent amount itself. The multiplier for the company is two.
That is the cap on the penalty for every OFFICER in default, whose penalty is one-tenth of the amount or ₹2 lakh, whichever is less.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 136(1) · Circulation of financial statements
questions.stem: A copy of the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statement, the auditor's report and every other document required by law to be annexed or attached, must be sent to every member of the company:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 136(1)

readLink.label: Read: Right to copies — s. 136 →

options.text: Not less than seven days before the date of the general meeting
options.explanation: Seven days is the s. 17 period for supplying copies of the memorandum and articles on request, not the s. 136 circulation period.

options.text: Not less than fourteen days before the date of the general meeting
options.explanation: Twenty-one days is the notice period for a general meeting and the circulation period under s. 136 alike; fourteen days appears nowhere here.

options.text: Not less than twenty-one days before the date of the general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 136(1) requires circulation not less than twenty-one days before the meeting, to every member, every trustee for the debenture-holders and all other persons entitled to notice.

options.text: On or before the date of the general meeting
options.explanation: Circulation at the meeting itself defeats the purpose of the section, which is to let members read the accounts in advance.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 136(1) proviso · The 95% relaxation
questions.stem: Where the documents referred to in section 136(1) are sent less than twenty-one days before the general meeting of a company having a share capital, they are deemed to have been duly sent if it is so agreed by members:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, first proviso to s. 136(1)

readLink.label: Read: Right to copies — s. 136 →

options.text: Holding not less than seventy-five per cent of the paid-up share capital giving a right to vote
options.explanation: Seventy-five per cent is the special-resolution majority. The proviso requires ninety-five per cent, and a majority in number as well.

options.text: Being a majority in number entitled to vote and representing not less than ninety-five per cent of such part of the paid-up share capital of the company as gives a right to vote
options.explanation: Correct. Both tests must be satisfied together — a majority in NUMBER, and ninety-five per cent of the voting paid-up share capital.

options.text: Being a majority in number entitled to vote, whatever the extent of their shareholding
options.explanation: This drops the ninety-five per cent capital test, which is the harder of the two.

options.text: Present in person at the meeting and representing not less than ninety per cent of the paid-up share capital
options.explanation: The agreement is not confined to members present in person, and the figure is ninety-five per cent, not ninety.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 137(1) · Filing after the AGM
questions.stem: The annual general meeting of Girikand Papers Limited is held on 22 August 2026 and the financial statements are duly adopted at it. The last date for filing them with the Registrar under section 137(1) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 137(1) — 30 days from the date of the annual general meeting

readLink.label: Read: Filing with the Registrar — s. 137 →

options.text: 21 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days counted from (and excluding) 22 August 2026 ends on 21 September 2026.

options.text: 22 September 2026
options.explanation: This treats the period as one calendar month, or counts the day of the meeting as day one.

options.text: 21 October 2026
options.explanation: That is sixty days. Section 137(1) allows thirty.

options.text: 20 November 2026
options.explanation: That is ninety days, which appears nowhere in s. 137.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 137(2) · Filing where no AGM is held
questions.stem: Suvarna Cables Limited, whose financial year ended on 31 March 2026, held no annual general meeting at all. The last date before which its annual general meeting ought to have been held was 30 September 2026. The financial statements, the documents required to be attached and the reasons for not holding the meeting must be filed with the Registrar by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 137(2) — 30 days from the last date before which the AGM should have been held

readLink.label: Read: Filing with the Registrar — s. 137 →

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.explanation: That is the last date for holding the meeting itself. The filing clock begins on that date; it does not end on it.

options.text: 29 October 2026
options.explanation: This counts 30 September as day one — the usual off-by-one.

options.text: 30 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days counted from (and excluding) 30 September 2026 ends on 30 October 2026.

options.text: 29 December 2026
options.explanation: That is ninety days. No ninety-day period exists in s. 137.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 138 · Unlisted public company threshold
questions.stem: During the preceding financial year Hiranya Alloys Limited, an unlisted public company, had a paid-up share capital of ₹38 crore, a turnover of ₹165 crore, outstanding borrowings from a bank that touched ₹120 crore in October, and outstanding deposits of ₹9 crore. In relation to internal audit under section 138:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Internal audit — s. 138 →

options.text: Internal audit is not required, none of the prescribed criteria having been met
options.explanation: One criterion was met. The borrowings from a bank exceeded ₹100 crore at a point of time during the preceding financial year.

options.text: Internal audit is required, the turnover criterion having been met
options.explanation: The turnover is ₹165 crore, below the ₹200 crore limb for an unlisted public company.

options.text: Internal audit is required, the outstanding-borrowings criterion having been met
options.explanation: Correct. Borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding ₹100 crore at ANY point of time during the preceding financial year trigger the requirement, and ₹120 crore does so.

options.text: Internal audit is required, the paid-up share capital criterion having been met
options.explanation: The paid-up share capital is ₹38 crore, below the ₹50 crore limb.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 138 · Private company threshold
questions.stem: During the preceding financial year Chandrika Papers Private Limited had a paid-up share capital of ₹70 crore, a turnover of ₹90 crore, no outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions, and outstanding deposits of ₹30 crore. In relation to internal audit under section 138:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Internal audit — s. 138 →

options.text: Internal audit is required, the paid-up share capital criterion having been met
options.explanation: There is no paid-up share capital limb for a private company; that limb applies only to an unlisted PUBLIC company.

options.text: Internal audit is required, the deposits criterion having been met
options.explanation: There is no deposits limb for a private company either; the ₹25 crore deposits limb applies only to an unlisted public company.

options.text: Internal audit is required, both the paid-up share capital and the deposits criteria having been met
options.explanation: Both of the limbs relied on are unavailable to a private company, so combining them changes nothing.

options.text: Internal audit is not required, a private company being tested only on turnover of ₹200 crore or more and on outstanding loans or borrowings exceeding ₹100 crore, neither of which is met
options.explanation: Correct. For a private company only two limbs exist — turnover ₹200 crore and borrowings above ₹100 crore. Turnover is ₹90 crore and there are no borrowings, so nothing is triggered.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 128 · Books of account
questions.stem: Explain the requirements of section 128 of the Companies Act 2013 relating to the maintenance, location, inspection and preservation of the books of account of a company, and state who is answerable for a default. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 128(1): every company shall prepare and keep at its registered office books of account, other relevant books and papers and the financial statement for every financial year, which give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company including that of its branch offices, and explain the transactions effected both at the registered office and at the branches
The books shall be kept on accrual basis and according to the double entry system of accounting

First proviso: all or any of the books may be kept at such other place in India as the Board of Directors may decide, and where such a decision is taken the company shall, within seven days of it, file with the Registrar a notice in writing giving the full address of that other place. Second proviso: the books and other relevant papers may be kept in electronic mode in the prescribed manner
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, provisos to s. 128(1); Rule 3, Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014 (rules-level)

skeleton.point: Section 128(2): where the company has a branch office in India or outside India, it is deemed to have complied if proper books of account relating to the transactions effected at the branch are kept at that office and proper summarised returns are sent periodically to the company at its registered office or at the other place referred to in section 128(1)

Sections 128(3) and (4): the books and papers maintained within India are open for inspection at the registered office or at that other place in India by any director during business hours; where financial information is maintained outside the country, copies of it must be maintained and produced for inspection by any director on the prescribed conditions; and the officers and employees must give the person making the inspection all reasonable assistance

Section 128(5): the books relating to a period of not less than eight financial years immediately preceding a financial year, together with the vouchers relevant to any entry in them, shall be kept in good order — or, where the company has been in existence for less than eight years, for all the preceding years; and where an investigation has been ordered under Chapter XIV the Central Government may direct that they be kept for such longer period as it may deem fit
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 128(5) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Section 128(6): the managing director, the whole-time director in charge of finance, the Chief Financial Officer or any other person of the company charged by the Board with the duty of complying with the section is liable, on contravention, to a penalty of ₹50,000

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 129 · Financial statements and consolidation
questions.stem: State the requirements of section 129 of the Companies Act 2013 as to the form and content of financial statements, and explain when and how a company must prepare consolidated financial statements. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 129(1): the financial statements shall give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company or companies, comply with the accounting standards notified under section 133, and be in the form or forms provided for different classes of companies in Schedule III; the proviso disapplies the Schedule III form to insurance companies, banking companies, companies engaged in the generation or supply of electricity and any other class governed by a special Act, to the extent that Act provides
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 129(1) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Section 129(2): the Board of Directors shall lay the financial statements at every annual general meeting of the company

Section 129(3): where a company has one or more subsidiaries or associate companies, it shall, in addition to its own financial statements, prepare a consolidated financial statement of the company and of all the subsidiaries and associates in the same form and manner as its own, and lay it before the annual general meeting along with its own financial statements

Proviso to section 129(3): the company shall also attach a statement containing the salient features of the financial statement of each subsidiary and associate, in the prescribed form (Form AOC-1). Explanation: for this purpose the word 'subsidiary' includes an associate company and a joint venture
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, proviso and Explanation to s. 129(3); Form AOC-1 (rules-level)

skeleton.point: Section 129(4): the provisions applicable to the preparation, adoption, audit and filing of a company's financial statements apply mutatis mutandis to the consolidated financial statement. Section 129(5): where the financial statements do not comply with the accounting standards, the company shall disclose the deviation, the reasons for it and the financial effects, if any, arising from it. Section 129(6): the Central Government may, on its own or on application, exempt a class of companies from any requirement of the section in the public interest

Section 129(7): on contravention the managing director, the whole-time director in charge of finance, the Chief Financial Officer, any other person charged by the Board with the duty of complying and, in the absence of any of them, all the directors are liable to imprisonment or fine or both as the sub-section provides

questions.topic: Ch 9 · ss. 130 and 131 · Reopening and voluntary revision
questions.stem: Distinguish between the re-opening of accounts on a court's or the Tribunal's order under section 130 and the voluntary revision of financial statements or the Board's report under section 131 of the Companies Act 2013. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 130: a company shall not re-open its books of account and shall not re-cast its financial statements unless an application in that behalf is made by the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board, any other statutory regulatory body or authority or any person concerned, and an order is made by a court of competent jurisdiction or by the Tribunal

The grounds are that the relevant earlier accounts were prepared in a fraudulent manner, or that the affairs of the company were mismanaged during the relevant period casting a doubt on the reliability of the financial statements; the court or Tribunal must give notice to the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board or any other statutory regulatory body concerned and any other person concerned and consider their representations; and under section 130(2) the accounts so revised or re-cast are final
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 130(1) proviso and s. 130(2)

skeleton.point: Section 130(3): no order shall be made in respect of re-opening books of account relating to a period earlier than the eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year, unless a direction has been issued under section 128(5) for keeping the books for a longer period, in which case they may be ordered to be re-opened within that longer period
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 130(3) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Section 131: where it appears to the DIRECTORS that the financial statement or the report of the Board does not comply with section 129 or section 134, they may prepare a revised financial statement or a revised report in respect of any of the three preceding financial years, after obtaining the approval of the Tribunal on an application made by the company; the Tribunal gives notice to the Central Government and the income-tax authorities and considers their representations

Such revised financial statement or report shall not be prepared or filed more than once in a financial year, the detailed reasons for the revision must be disclosed in the Board's report of the year in which the revision is made, and where copies of the previous documents have already been sent to members, delivered to the Registrar or laid in general meeting, the revision must be confined to the correction for the non-compliance and to necessary consequential alterations
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, proviso to s. 131(1) and s. 131(2)

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 134 · Signing of accounts and the Board's report
questions.stem: Explain the requirements of section 134 of the Companies Act 2013 as to the approval and signing of financial statements, the contents of the Board's report, and the Directors' Responsibility Statement. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 134(1): the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statement if any, shall be approved by the Board of Directors before they are signed on behalf of the Board at least by the chairperson of the company where he is authorised by the Board, or by two directors of whom one shall be the managing director, and by the Chief Executive Officer if he is a director, the Chief Financial Officer and the company secretary of the company, wherever they are appointed; in the case of a One Person Company the financial statements are signed by only one director
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 134(1) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Section 134(2): the auditor's report shall be attached to every financial statement

Section 134(3): the Board's report attached to the financial statements shall include, among other matters, the web address where the annual return referred to in section 92(3) has been placed; the number of meetings of the Board; the Directors' Responsibility Statement; details of frauds reported by auditors under section 143(12) other than those reportable to the Central Government; a statement on the declaration given by independent directors; the remuneration policy for companies covered by section 178(1); explanations by the Board on every qualification, reservation, adverse remark or disclaimer in the auditor's report and the secretarial audit report; particulars of loans, guarantees and investments under section 186; particulars of related-party contracts under section 188(1); the state of the company's affairs; amounts carried to reserves; the dividend recommended; material changes and commitments affecting the financial position between the end of the financial year and the date of the report; conservation of energy, technology absorption and foreign exchange earnings and outgo; the risk management policy; and the development and implementation of the corporate social responsibility policy

Section 134(5) — the Directors' Responsibility Statement shall state that the applicable accounting standards were followed with proper explanation relating to material departures; that the directors selected accounting policies and applied them consistently and made judgments and estimates that are reasonable and prudent so as to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs and of the profit or loss; that they took proper and sufficient care for the maintenance of adequate accounting records for safeguarding the assets and for preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities; that they prepared the annual accounts on a going concern basis; that, in the case of a listed company, internal financial controls were laid down and are adequate and operating effectively; and that proper systems were devised to ensure compliance with all applicable laws and are adequate and operating effectively

Section 134(6): the Board's report and any annexures to it shall be signed by the chairperson of the company if he is authorised by the Board and, where he is not so authorised, by at least two directors one of whom shall be a managing director, or by the director where there is only one director
Section 134(8): on contravention the company is liable to a penalty of ₹3,00,000 and every officer of the company who is in default to a penalty of ₹50,000

questions.topic: Ch 9 · s. 135 · Corporate social responsibility
questions.stem: State the companies to which section 135 of the Companies Act 2013 applies, the constitution and functions of the Corporate Social Responsibility Committee, the amount a company must spend, and the treatment of any unspent amount. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 135(1): the section applies to every company having, during the immediately preceding financial year, a net worth of ₹500 crore or more, or a turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or a net profit of ₹5 crore or more — the three criteria being alternatives, so that any one of them brings the company within the section

Such a company shall constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board consisting of three or more directors, out of which at least one shall be an independent director; where the company is not required to appoint an independent director under section 149(4) it shall have two or more directors on the committee, and a private company having only two directors constitutes the committee with those two. Under section 135(9), where the amount to be spent under section 135(5) does not exceed ₹50 lakh, the requirement to constitute the committee does not apply and its functions are discharged by the Board of Directors
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(1) with its provisos, and s. 135(9)

skeleton.point: Sections 135(2), (3) and (4): the Board's report discloses the composition of the committee; the committee formulates and recommends to the Board a corporate social responsibility policy indicating the activities to be undertaken as specified in Schedule VII, recommends the amount of expenditure to be incurred, and monitors the policy from time to time; the Board approves the policy, discloses its contents in its report, places it on the company's website, and ensures that the activities included in the policy are actually undertaken

Section 135(5): the Board shall ensure that the company spends, in every financial year, at least two per cent of the average net profits of the company made during the three immediately preceding financial years, in pursuance of its policy; where the company has not completed three financial years since incorporation the average is taken over such financial years as have been completed; preference is to be given to the local area and areas around it where the company operates; and 'net profit' is calculated in accordance with section 198
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(5) with its first proviso and Explanation; s. 198

skeleton.point: Section 135(6): any amount remaining unspent pursuant to an ongoing project fulfilling the prescribed conditions shall be transferred, within thirty days from the end of the financial year, to a special account opened in any scheduled bank called the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account for that financial year; it shall be spent in pursuance of the policy within three financial years from the date of transfer, failing which it shall be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within thirty days from the completion of the third financial year

Second proviso to section 135(5): where the unspent amount does not relate to an ongoing project, the Board shall specify the reasons for not spending in its report under section 134(3)(o) and transfer the unspent amount to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year; and under the third proviso an amount spent in excess of the requirement may be set off against the requirement to spend for up to the three immediately succeeding financial years, subject to the prescribed conditions
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, second and third provisos to s. 135(5)

skeleton.point: Section 135(7): for default in complying with section 135(5) or (6) the company is liable to a penalty of twice the amount required to be transferred to the Fund specified in Schedule VII or to the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account, or ₹1 crore, whichever is less; and every officer in default to one-tenth of that amount or ₹2 lakh, whichever is less

questions.topic: Ch 9 · ss. 136, 137 and 138 · Copies, filing and internal audit
questions.stem: Explain the right of members to copies of the audited financial statements under section 136, the time limits for filing financial statements with the Registrar under section 137, and the classes of companies required to appoint an internal auditor under section 138. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 136(1): a copy of the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statement if any, the auditor's report and every other document required by law to be annexed or attached shall be sent to every member, to every trustee for the debenture-holders and to all other persons entitled to receive notice of the general meeting, not less than twenty-one days before the date of the meeting; where they are sent less than twenty-one days before, they are deemed duly sent if so agreed by members being a majority in number entitled to vote and representing not less than ninety-five per cent of such part of the paid-up share capital as gives a right to vote, or, where the company has no share capital, by members having not less than ninety-five per cent of the total voting power
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 136(1) and its first proviso

skeleton.point: A listed company is deemed to comply if copies are kept for inspection at the registered office during working hours for twenty-one days before the meeting and a statement containing the salient features of the documents in the prescribed form, or copies of the documents, is sent twenty-one days before; it must also place the documents on its website and, if it has a subsidiary, place that subsidiary's separate audited accounts on the website and give a copy to any shareholder who asks. Section 136(2) requires inspection at the registered office during business hours, and section 136(3) imposes a penalty of ₹25,000 on the company and ₹5,000 on every officer in default
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 136(1) provisos, s. 136(2) and (3)

skeleton.point: Section 137(1): a copy of the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statement, along with all the documents required to be attached, duly adopted at the annual general meeting, shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the date of the meeting; where they are not adopted at the annual general meeting or at the adjourned meeting, they shall be filed within thirty days of the date of the annual general meeting and the Registrar shall take them in his records as provisional, the adopted statements being filed within thirty days of the date of the adjourned meeting; and a One Person Company shall file the financial statements duly adopted by its member within one hundred and eighty days from the closure of the financial year
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 137(1) with its provisos

skeleton.point: Section 137(2): where the annual general meeting has not been held, the financial statements along with the documents required to be attached and the reasons for not holding the meeting shall be filed within thirty days of the last date before which the meeting should have been held. Section 137(3): the company is liable to a penalty of ₹10,000 with a further ₹100 for each day of continuing failure subject to ₹2,00,000, and the managing director and the Chief Financial Officer (or the director charged by the Board, or in the absence of any such director all the directors) to ₹10,000 with a further ₹100 per day subject to ₹50,000

Section 138 read with the prescribed rules: an internal auditor must be appointed by every listed company; every unlisted public company having, during the preceding financial year, paid-up share capital of ₹50 crore or more, or turnover of ₹200 crore or more, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding ₹100 crore at any point of time, or outstanding deposits of ₹25 crore or more at any point of time; and every private company having, during the preceding financial year, turnover of ₹200 crore or more, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding ₹100 crore at any point of time
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 138(1); Rule 13, Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014 (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)

skeleton.point: The internal auditor shall be a chartered accountant or a cost accountant, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board, and may or may not be an employee of the company; the Audit Committee, or the Board where there is no Audit Committee, shall in consultation with the internal auditor formulate the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology for conducting the internal audit

questions.topic: Ch 9 · Case: a CSR obligation from applicability to penalty
questions.case: Anantara Speciality Chemicals Limited is an unlisted public company that is not required to appoint an independent director. For the financial year 2025-26 its net worth was ₹612 crore, its turnover ₹740 crore and its net profit ₹4.10 crore. Its net profits computed in accordance with section 198 were ₹6.20 crore for 2023-24, ₹9.40 crore for 2024-25 and ₹4.20 crore for 2025-26. The company's financial year 2026-27 ends on 31 March 2027. During 2026-27 it actually spends ₹5,20,000 on activities in Schedule VII. Of the shortfall, ₹6,00,000 is attributable to a school-building project already approved by the Board as an ongoing project, and ₹2,00,000 is not attributable to any ongoing project.

readLink.label: Read: CSR spend, unspent amounts and penalty →

questions.stem: The amount that the Board must ensure Anantara Speciality Chemicals Limited spends on corporate social responsibility for the financial year 2026-27 is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(5) — 2% of the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years

options.explanation: Correct. The three-year total is ₹19.80 crore, the average ₹6.60 crore, and 2% of ₹6,60,00,000 is ₹13,20,000.
This is 2% of the latest year's net profit of ₹4.20 crore. The obligation is measured on a three-year average.
This is 2% of the TOTAL of the three years, which triples the correct figure.
This is 1% of the average. The statutory rate is two per cent.

questions.stem: In relation to the constitution of a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee, Anantara Speciality Chemicals Limited must:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 135(1) with its provisos, and s. 135(9)

options.text: Constitute a committee of three or more directors, at least one of whom is an independent director
options.explanation: That is the default rule, and it is displaced twice over here — the company is not required to appoint an independent director, and its obligation is below ₹50 lakh.

options.text: Constitute a committee of two or more directors, being a company that is not required to appoint an independent director
options.explanation: This would be right if the amount to be spent exceeded ₹50 lakh. It does not, so section 135(9) removes the committee requirement altogether.

options.text: Not constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee at all, because the amount to be spent under section 135(5) does not exceed ₹50 lakh, the functions of the committee being discharged by the Board of Directors
options.explanation: Correct. The obligation of ₹13,20,000 is below ₹50 lakh, so section 135(9) applies and the Board discharges the committee's functions.

options.text: Not constitute a committee, and it is also relieved of the obligation to spend, the amount being below ₹50 lakh
options.explanation: Section 135(9) removes only the COMMITTEE. The obligation to spend two per cent, and the consequences of not spending, are untouched.

questions.stem: The ₹2,00,000 that is not attributable to any ongoing project must be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, second proviso to s. 135(5) — 6 months from the expiry of the financial year

options.text: 30 April 2027
options.explanation: That is thirty days from the end of the financial year, which is the clock for an ONGOING-PROJECT amount going into the company's own Unspent CSR Account.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Six months from the expiry of the financial year on 31 March 2027 ends on 30 September 2027.

options.text: 30 June 2027
options.explanation: Three calendar months from the end of the financial year is not a period recognised anywhere in section 135.

options.text: 31 March 2030
options.explanation: That is the end of the three-financial-year window under section 135(6), which applies only to money in the Unspent CSR Account.

questions.stem: Suppose instead that Anantara Speciality Chemicals Limited had spent ₹20,00,000 during the financial year 2026-27. The excess of ₹6,80,000 may be:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, third proviso to s. 135(5)

options.text: Set off against the requirement to spend under section 135(5) for up to the three immediately succeeding financial years, subject to the prescribed conditions
options.explanation: Correct. The third proviso to section 135(5) permits a forward set-off for up to three immediately succeeding financial years, on the conditions prescribed by the Rules.

options.text: Refunded to the company out of a Fund specified in Schedule VII
options.explanation: Nothing in section 135 provides for a refund from any Fund.

options.text: Carried back and set off against a shortfall of the immediately preceding financial year
options.explanation: The set-off runs forward only; there is no carry-back.

options.text: Retained without any consequence, no set-off being permitted under the Act
options.explanation: A set-off IS permitted. Denying it makes the third proviso to section 135(5) meaningless.

questions.topic: Ch 9 · Case: three filing clocks from one financial year
questions.case: Three companies close their financial year on 31 March 2026. Vrinda Agro Foods Private Limited holds its annual general meeting on 18 September 2026, but the members adjourn the meeting without adopting the financial statements. Suvarna Cables Limited holds no annual general meeting at all; the last date before which its meeting ought to have been held is 30 September 2026. Kalash Ventures (OPC) Private Limited, a One Person Company, has its financial statements adopted by its single member on 2 August 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Filing with the Registrar — s. 137 →

questions.stem: The last date for Kalash Ventures (OPC) Private Limited to file its financial statements with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, proviso to s. 137(1) — 180 days from the closure of the financial year

options.text: 27 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. One hundred and eighty days counted from (and excluding) 31 March 2026 ends on 27 September 2026; the date on which the member adopted the accounts is irrelevant to the clock.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.explanation: This treats the period as six calendar months. The proviso speaks of one hundred and eighty days.

options.text: 26 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts 31 March itself as day one — the usual off-by-one.

options.text: 1 September 2026
options.explanation: This runs thirty days from the date of adoption by the member. For a One Person Company the clock starts at the CLOSURE OF THE FINANCIAL YEAR, and it runs for one hundred and eighty days.

questions.stem: The last date for Vrinda Agro Foods Private Limited to file its unadopted financial statements with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, first proviso to s. 137(1) — 30 days from the date of the annual general meeting

options.text: 3 October 2026
options.explanation: That is fifteen days. No fifteen-day period exists in section 137.

options.text: 17 October 2026
options.explanation: This counts 18 September as day one — the usual off-by-one.

options.text: 18 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days counted from (and excluding) the date of the annual general meeting, 18 September 2026, ends on 18 October 2026.

options.text: 17 December 2026
options.explanation: That is ninety days, which appears nowhere in section 137.

questions.stem: The financial statements that Vrinda Agro Foods Private Limited files without adoption are:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, first proviso to s. 137(1)

options.text: Not required to be filed at all until they are adopted at the adjourned annual general meeting
options.explanation: The filing is mandatory. Failure to adopt is no excuse for failure to file within thirty days of the meeting.

options.text: Taken in the Registrar's records as provisional, the adopted financial statements being filed within thirty days of the date of the adjourned annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso makes the first filing provisional and starts a fresh thirty-day clock from the adjourned meeting at which the statements are adopted.

options.text: Taken in the Registrar's records as final, no further filing being required after adoption
options.explanation: The provisional filing does not discharge the obligation; the adopted statements must follow.

options.text: Required to be filed within one hundred and eighty days of the closure of the financial year, the company being a private company
